implementation_notes: Guava implements the pattern literally: Range<C extends Comparable> is immutable, and the nine bound combinations come from closed, closedOpen, open, openClosed, greaterThan, atLeast, lessThan, atMost and all; contains, containsAll, encloses, isConnected, intersection, span and (since 27.0) gap form the query surface, and DiscreteDomain plus ContiguousSet.create turn a range over a discrete type into an enumerable set with canonical() normalising equivalent forms. The JDK itself has no interval value - IntStream.range/rangeClosed only enumerate integers - so Guava Range is the default Java realization, with RangeSet/RangeMap for collections of intervals.
pitfalls: intersection and gap throw IllegalArgumentException for disconnected ranges; test isConnected first or the exception surfaces deep in domain code.

Equality is structural, not set-based: [3..3), (3..3] and (4..4] are all empty yet pairwise unequal, and (1..4) is not equal to [2..3] over integers unless canonical(DiscreteDomain) is applied - so deduplicating or keying maps on Range needs the canonical form.
Range implements Predicate<C>, which makes it easy to pass a range into stream filters and lose the interval operations that the caller actually needed.

For temporal ranges the discrete-domain machinery does not apply: dates are not a DiscreteDomain, so enumerating a Range<LocalDate> requires ContiguousSet over LocalDate only if you supply a domain, otherwise iterate from the endpoints explicitly.

variants.name: ThreeTen-Extra Interval over java.time.Instant
variants.implementation_notes: For instant-based ranges ThreeTen-Extra supplies an immutable Interval whose start is inclusive and end exclusive, with unbounded ends (ALL, startingAt, endingAt, parse) and the operations abuts, connected, encloses, intersects, overlaps, isEmpty, intersection, union and span - the java.time-based successor of Joda-Time's Interval. Choose it when the domain is a timeline of instants and windows are half-open by nature; keep Guava Range when the domain is an arbitrary Comparable such as a version or an integer tier.
pitfalls: The bound convention is fixed (start inclusive, end exclusive); a closed business period needs an explicit decision about the final nanosecond or day, and endingAt is also open.
Intervals are documented as not comparable: comparing two of them means comparing getDuration(), so they cannot be used directly in sorted collections.
Interval.ALL and unbounded intervals interact with intersection and union results, so callers must handle the unbounded case instead of assuming concrete endpoints.
